title: Part 2, Chapter 63
paragraphs: About the mishap that befell Sancho Panza through his visit to the galleys, and the strange adventure of the fair Morisco

Don Quixote's thoughts ran deep on the enchanted head's reply, though none of them landed anywhere near the secret of the trick — all of them concentrated instead on the promise, which he treated as a certainty, of Dulcinea's disenchantment. He turned this over in his mind with great satisfaction, fully persuaded he would shortly see it come true; and as for Sancho, though, as has been said, he hated being a governor, he still had a hankering to give orders and be obeyed once more. This is the misfortune that comes with authority, even in jest.

To pick up the thread: that afternoon their host Don Antonio Moreno and his two friends, with Don Quixote and Sancho, went to the galleys. The commandant had already been told of his good fortune in seeing two such famous persons as Don Quixote and Sancho, and the instant they came to the shore all the galleys struck their awnings and the trumpets rang out. A skiff covered with rich carpets and crimson velvet cushions was lowered into the water, and as Don Quixote stepped on board the leading galley fired her gangway gun, and the other galleys did the same. As he mounted the starboard ladder the whole crew saluted him (as is the custom when a distinguished person comes on board a galley) by shouting "Hu, hu, hu," three times. The general — for so we shall call him, a Valencian gentleman of rank — gave him his hand, embraced him, and said, "I shall mark this day with a white stone as one of the happiest I can ever expect, since I have seen Señor Don Quixote of La Mancha, the pattern and image in whom is contained and condensed all that is worthy in knight-errantry."

Don Quixote, delighted beyond measure with such a lordly reception, replied in words no less courteous. They all proceeded to the poop, which was handsomely decorated, and seated themselves on the bulwark benches. The boatswain went along the gangway and piped all hands to strip, which they did in an instant. Sancho, seeing so many men stripped to the skin, was taken aback, and even more so when he saw them spread the awning so briskly that it seemed to him all the devils were at work on it. But all this was cakes and fancy bread compared to what I am about to tell. Sancho was seated on the captain's stage, close to the aftermost rower on the right-hand side. He, briefed in advance on what to do, took hold of Sancho, hoisted him up in his arms, and the whole crew, who were standing ready, beginning on the right, passed him along, whirling him from hand to hand and bench to bench with such speed that it took the sight out of poor Sancho's eyes. He was quite sure the devils themselves were flying off with him. They did not leave off until they had sent him back along the left side and deposited him on the poop, and the poor man was left bruised, breathless, drenched in sweat, and unable to grasp what had just happened to him.

When Don Quixote saw Sancho's flight without wings, he asked the general whether this was a usual ceremony for newcomers on board the galleys; because, if so, since he had no intention of adopting it as a profession, he had no mind to perform such feats of agility, and if anyone tried to grab hold of him to whirl him about, he swore to God he would kick his soul out. As he said this he stood up and clapped his hand on his sword. Just then they struck the awning and lowered the yard with an enormous rattle. Sancho thought heaven was coming off its hinges and about to fall on his head, and in his terror he ducked it and buried it between his knees. Don Quixote's knees were not entirely under control either — he too shook a little, hunched his shoulders, and lost colour. The crew then hoisted the yard with the same speed and clatter, all the while keeping silence as if they had neither voice nor breath. The boatswain gave the signal to weigh anchor, and leaping onto the middle of the gangway began to lay on to the shoulders of the crew with his whip, and gradually hauled the ship out to sea.

When Sancho saw so many red feet (for that's what he took the oars to be) moving all together, he said to himself, "It's these that are the real enchanted things, not the ones my master goes on about. What can those wretches have done to be so whipped — and how does that one man strolling along whistling dare to whip so many? I declare, this is hell, or at the very least purgatory!"

Don Quixote, observing how attentively Sancho watched what was going on, said to him, "Ah, Sancho my friend, how quickly and cheaply you could finish off Dulcinea's disenchantment if you'd strip to the waist and take your place among those gentlemen! Surrounded by the pain and suffering of so many, you wouldn't feel your own much; and besides, perhaps the sage Merlin would allow each of these lashes, laid on with a good hand, to count for ten of the ones you must give yourself in the end."
The general was about to ask what these lashes were, and what Dulcinea's disenchantment was, when a sailor shouted, "Monjui signals that there is an oared vessel off the coast to the west."

On hearing this the general sprang onto the gangway crying, "Now then, my sons, don't let her give us the slip! It must be some Algerine corsair brigantine that the watchtower is signalling." The three other galleys immediately came alongside the chief galley for their orders. The general sent two out to sea while he kept inshore with the other, so the vessel could not escape. The crews plied the oars so furiously that the galleys seemed to fly. The two that had put out to sea, after a couple of miles, sighted a vessel which, as far as they could tell, they judged to be one of fourteen or fifteen banks of oars — and so she proved. As soon as the vessel spotted the galleys she went about, hoping to escape on her speed; but the attempt failed, for the chief galley was one of the fastest vessels afloat and overhauled her so quickly that those on board the brigantine saw there was no possibility of escape. The rais would have had them drop their oars and surrender so as not to provoke the captain in command. But chance ordered things otherwise. Just as the chief galley came close enough for those on board to hear the shouts calling on them to surrender, two Toraquis — that is to say two Turks — both drunk, who with a dozen more were on board the brigantine, fired their muskets and killed two of the soldiers lining the sides of our vessel. Seeing this the general swore he would not leave a single man alive among those on board, but as he bore down furiously on her she slipped out from under his oars. The galley shot well ahead; those on board the vessel saw their case was desperate, and while the galley was coming about they made sail, and by sailing and rowing tried once more to get away. Their effort did them less good than their rashness did them harm, for the galley caught up with them in a little more than half a mile, threw her oars over them, and took the whole crew alive. The other two galleys now joined company and all four returned with the prize to the beach, where a vast crowd stood waiting, eager to see what they had brought back. The general anchored close in, and saw that the viceroy of the city was on the shore. He ordered the skiff to push off to fetch him, and the yard to be lowered so as to hang at once the rais and the rest of the men taken on board the vessel — about thirty-six in number, all smart fellows and most of them Turkish musketeers. He asked which was the rais of the brigantine, and was answered in Spanish by one of the prisoners (who afterwards proved to be a Spanish renegade), "This young man, señor, that you see here is our rais," pointing to one of the handsomest and most gallant-looking youths imaginable. He did not look twenty years old.

"Tell me, dog," said the general, "what led you to kill my soldiers, when you saw it was impossible for you to escape? Is that how to behave to a chief galley? Don't you know that rashness is not valour? Faint prospects of success should make men bold, not reckless."

The rais was about to reply, but the general couldn't listen at that moment, as he had to hurry to receive the viceroy, who was now coming on board the galley with some of his attendants and some of the local people.
"You've had a good chase, señor general," said the viceroy.
"Your excellency shall soon see how good, by the game strung up to this yard," replied the general.
"How so?" asked the viceroy.

"Because," said the general, "against all law, reason, and the usages of war, they have killed on my hands two of the best soldiers on board these galleys, and I have sworn to hang every man I took — but above all this youth, who is the rais of the brigantine." And he pointed to him as he stood with his hands already bound and the rope around his neck, ready for death.

The viceroy looked at him, and seeing him so well-favoured, so graceful, and so submissive, felt a desire to spare his life — the youth's good looks acting at once as a letter of recommendation. He questioned him, saying, "Tell me, rais, are you Turk, Moor, or renegade?"
The youth replied, also in Spanish, "I am neither Turk, nor Moor, nor renegade."
"What are you, then?" said the viceroy.
"A Christian woman," replied the youth.
"A woman and a Christian, in such a dress and in such circumstances! That is more marvellous than credible," said the viceroy.
"Suspend the execution of the sentence," said the youth; "your vengeance will not lose much by waiting while I tell you the story of my life."

What heart could be so hard as not to soften at these words, at least enough to listen to what the unhappy youth had to say? The general told her to say what she pleased, but not to expect pardon for her flagrant offence. With this permission the youth began as follows.

"Born of Morisco parents, I am of that nation — more unhappy than wise — on which a sea of woes has lately poured down. In the course of our misfortunes I was carried off to Barbary by two uncles of mine, for it was useless to declare that I was a Christian, as in fact I am — and not a pretended or merely outward one, but a true Catholic Christian. It did me no good with those in charge of our sad expatriation to protest this, nor would my uncles believe it; on the contrary, they treated it as a lie and a ruse to let me stay behind in the land of my birth. And so, more by force than by my own will, they took me with them. I had a Christian mother, and a father who was a sensible man and a Christian too. I drank in the Catholic faith with my mother's milk, I was well brought up, and in neither word nor deed did I, I think, show any sign of being a Morisco. To match those virtues — for that is what I hold them to be — my beauty, if I have any, grew along with me; and great as was the seclusion in which I lived, it was not so great that a young gentleman, Don Gaspar Gregorio by name, eldest son of a gentleman who is lord of a village near ours, did not contrive to find opportunities of seeing me. How he saw me, how we met, how his heart was lost to me and mine not kept from him, would take too long to tell, especially at a moment when I am in dread of the cruel cord that threatens to come between my tongue and my throat. I will only say, therefore, that Don Gregorio chose to come with me into exile. He joined the Moriscoes who were going forth from other villages, for he knew their language well, and on the voyage he struck up a friendship with the two uncles who were carrying me with them. My father, as a wise and far-sighted man, had as soon as he heard the first edict for our expulsion left the village and gone in search of some refuge for us abroad. He left hidden and buried, at a spot known only to me, a large quantity of pearls and precious stones of great value, together with a sum of money in gold cruzadoes and doubloons. He charged me on no account to touch the treasure, if by any chance they expelled us before his return. I obeyed him, and with my uncles, as I have said, and others of our kindred and neighbours, crossed over to Barbary, and the place we ended up was Algiers — much the same as if we had ended up in hell itself. The king heard of my beauty, and rumour told him of my wealth, which was in some respects fortunate for me. He summoned me before him, and asked me what part of Spain I came from, and what money and jewels I had. I told him the place, and told him the jewels and money were buried there but could easily be recovered if I went back for them myself. All this I said, fearing my beauty rather than his own greed might influence him. While he was talking with me, they brought him word that one of the handsomest and most graceful youths imaginable was travelling in my company. I knew at once they were speaking of Don Gaspar Gregorio, whose looks outdid the most highly praised beauty. I was alarmed when I thought of the danger he was in, for among those barbarous Turks a fair youth is more prized than any woman, however beautiful. The king at once ordered him to be brought before him so he could see him, and asked me if what they said about the youth was true. Then, almost as if inspired by heaven, I told him it was — but that he should know it was not a man but a woman like myself, and I begged him to let me go and dress her in the attire proper to her, so her beauty could be seen to perfection and so she could present herself before him with less embarrassment. He told me to go by all means, and said that the next day we would discuss the plan for my return to Spain to carry away the hidden treasure. I went to Don Gaspar, told him the danger he was in if he let it be seen he was a man, dressed him as a Moorish woman, and that same afternoon brought him before the king, who was charmed at the sight of him, and resolved to keep the damsel and make a present of her to the Grand Signor. To avoid the risk she might run among the women of his harem, and distrustful of himself, he ordered her to be placed in the house of some Moorish ladies of rank who would protect and attend to her — and there he was taken at once. What we both suffered (for I cannot deny that I love him) can be left to the imagination of those who have been separated from someone they love dearly. The king then arranged that I should return to Spain in this brigantine, and that two Turks — the ones who killed your soldiers — should come with me. With me there also came this Spanish renegade" — and here she pointed to the one who had first spoken — "whom I know to be secretly a Christian, and more eager to be left in Spain than to return to Barbary. The rest of the crew of the brigantine are Moors and Turks, who only serve as rowers. The two Turks, greedy and insolent, instead of obeying the orders we had to put me and this renegade ashore in Christian dress (which we came supplied with) on the first Spanish ground we touched, chose to run along the coast and take some prize if they could, fearing that if they landed us first we might, if some accident happened to us, make it known the brigantine was at sea, and that, if there were any galleys on the coast, they might be caught. We sighted this shore last night, and knowing nothing of these galleys, were discovered — and the result is what you have seen. To sum up: there is Don Gregorio in woman's dress, among women, in imminent danger of his life; and here am I, hands bound, expecting — or rather dreading — to lose a life I am already weary of. Here, sirs, ends my sad story, as true as it is unhappy. All I ask of you is to let me die like a Christian, for, as I have already said, I am not to be charged with the offence of which those of my nation are guilty." And she stood silent, her eyes filled with moving tears, joined by plenty from the bystanders. The viceroy, touched with compassion, went up to her without speaking and untied the cord that bound the Moorish girl's hands.

But all the while the Morisco Christian was telling her strange story, an elderly pilgrim who had come on board the galley at the same time as the viceroy had kept his eyes fixed on her; and the instant she finished speaking he threw himself at her feet, embraced them, and said in a voice broken by sobs and sighs, "O Ana Felix, my unhappy daughter! I am your father Ricote, come back to look for you, unable to live without you, my soul!"

At these words Sancho opened his eyes and raised his head, which he had been holding down, brooding over his unlucky excursion; and looking at the pilgrim he recognised in him that same Ricote he had met the day he left his government, and was satisfied that this was his daughter. Now unbound, she embraced her father, mingling her tears with his, while he, addressing the general and the viceroy, said, "This, sirs, is my daughter, more unhappy in her adventures than in her name. She is Ana Felix, surnamed Ricote, as celebrated for her beauty as for my wealth. I quit my native land in search of some shelter or refuge for us abroad, and having found one in Germany I returned in this pilgrim's dress, in company with some other German pilgrims, to look for my daughter and take up a large quantity of treasure I had left buried. My daughter I did not find; the treasure I found and have with me; and now, in this strange roundabout way you have seen, I find the treasure that, more than all the rest, makes me rich — my beloved daughter. If our innocence, and her tears and mine, can with strict justice open the door to clemency, extend it to us, for we never had any intention of injuring you, nor do we sympathise with the aims of our people, who have been justly banished."

"I know Ricote well," said Sancho at this, "and I know too that what he says about Ana Felix being his daughter is true; but as for those other particulars about going and coming, and having good or bad intentions, I say nothing."

While everyone stood amazed at this strange turn of events, the general said, "At any rate your tears won't allow me to keep my oath. Live, fair Ana Felix, all the years that heaven has allotted you; but these rash, insolent fellows must pay the penalty of the crime they committed." And with that he gave orders to have the two Turks who had killed his two soldiers hanged at once from the yard-arm. The viceroy, however, begged him earnestly not to hang them, since their behaviour smacked more of madness than of bravado. The general yielded to the viceroy's request, for revenge is not easily taken in cold blood. They then tried to devise some scheme for rescuing Don Gaspar Gregorio from the danger he had been left in. Ricote offered for that purpose more than two thousand ducats he had in pearls and gems; they discussed several plans, but none so good as the one suggested by the renegade already mentioned, who offered to return to Algiers in a small vessel of about six banks, manned by Christian rowers, since he knew where, how, and when he could and should land, and knew the house where Don Gaspar was staying. The general and the viceroy had some hesitation about trusting the renegade with the Christians who were to row, but Ana Felix said she could vouch for him, and her father offered to go and pay the Christians' ransom if for some reason they did not come back. That being settled, the viceroy landed, and Don Antonio Moreno took the fair Morisco and her father home with him, the viceroy charging him to give them the best reception and welcome he could, while on his own part he offered everything his house contained for their entertainment — so great was the good will and kindness Ana Felix's beauty had infused into his heart.
